analysis.one_liner: Tightens bank regulation to protect deposit insurance funds and taxpayers after the savings-and-loan crisis.
analysis.headline: Passed with broad bipartisan support and was signed into law in December 1991, overhauling bank supervision after the savings-and-loan crisis; the Senate cleared the final deal 68-15 and the House by voice vote.
analysis.plain_summary: After the savings-and-loan bailout cost taxpayers billions, this bill rewrote the rules for federally insured banks and thrifts. It forces regulators to step in early when a bank's finances deteriorate, requires yearly on-site exams, restricts risky deposit-gathering, and makes the FDIC close failed banks in the way that costs the insurance fund the least. It also raises the FDIC's line of credit at the Treasury from $5 billion to $30 billion with a required repayment schedule, and adds consumer rules like mandatory disclosure of savings account interest rates.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors get guaranteed coverage of up to $100,000 per account (plus extra coverage for certain retirement accounts), clear disclosure of what their savings accounts actually pay, and 30 days' notice before a branch closes. Taxpayers gain because regulators must act before a bank fails and the FDIC must resolve failures at the least long-term cost to the insurance fund. Small businesses and farms gain visibility through new annual lending reports from banks.

how_it_helps.text: Requires federal banking agencies to take 'prompt corrective action' on weak banks — capital restoration plans, growth limits, and receivership within 30 days when capital falls below critical levels — so problems are fixed before they drain the insurance fund [S2].

Directs the FDIC to resolve failed banks at the least possible long-term cost to the deposit insurance funds, and makes bank holding company affiliates liable to the FDIC for part of any loss [S2][S3].
Requires annual on-site examinations of insured institutions and more conservative, uniform accounting so a bank's true condition shows up early [S2][S3].

Creates the Truth in Savings Act, requiring banks to disclose interest rates and account terms, and sets up low-cost 'lifeline' basic transaction accounts with a reduced FDIC assessment for banks that offer them [S3].
Raises the FDIC's Treasury borrowing authority from $5 billion to $30 billion with a mandatory repayment schedule, so the insurance fund can cover failures without an emergency taxpayer bailout [S3].

Adds whistleblower protections for employees of troubled banks and of the banking regulators themselves, and requires uninsured institutions to tell customers clearly that their deposits are not federally insured [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks and thrifts bear the direct cost: higher insurance assessments, exam and supervision fees, stricter capital standards, growth limits and pay restrictions when undercapitalized, and tight limits on buying high-interest 'brokered' deposits. Some of those compliance costs are likely passed on to bank customers through fees and rates. Stricter capital rules can also make banks lend less during tight periods — Congress itself attached a statement urging steps to ease the early-1990s credit crunch.

drawbacks.text: The added assessments, exam fees, and compliance costs fall on insured institutions and are likely passed at least partly to customers through account fees and lower deposit rates [S3].

Forcing early closure of weak banks protects the insurance fund but can tighten credit in a downturn; Congress acknowledged this by adding a sense-of-the-House provision urging actions to arrest the 'credit crisis,' including easing capital treatment for real estate lending [S3].
Restrictions on brokered deposits limit banks' ability to compete for funds, which can reduce the interest rates paid to small savers, even though it lowers risk to the insurance fund [S2].
The enlarged $30 billion Treasury credit line means taxpayers remain the ultimate backstop for the banking system if bank failures exceed what the industry-funded insurance accounts can cover [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but widely judged worthwhile after the S&L disaster: taxpayers and depositors get much stronger protection against silent bank failures, while banks pay more and lose flexibility. The main honest caveats are that consumers bear some of the compliance cost and that the same early-intervention machinery can tighten credit in weak economies. A few thrift-friendly provisions, like loosening the qualified thrift lender test, trim the bill's discipline.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared both chambers, a House-Senate conference worked out the final version, both chambers agreed to it in late November 1991, and President George H.W. Bush signed it on December 19, 1991 as Public Law 102-242.

narrative.text: The Senate Banking Committee held seven days of hearings in April and May 1991 and reported the bill with a substitute amendment on October 1, 1991 [S5].

The Senate needed a cloture vote — a procedure requiring 60 senators to cut off delay — before it could take up the bill; that vote passed 76-19 on November 13, 1991 (Democrats 43-9, Republicans 33-10) [S6].
The Senate passed the bill by voice vote on November 21, 1991; the House instead inserted the text of its own companion bill, H.R. 3768, and both chambers went to conference [S5].
The House instructed its conferees to insist on replenishing the Bank Insurance Fund, agreeing 398-3 (Democrats 242-0, Republicans 155-3) [S7].

The Senate agreed to the conference report 68-15 on November 27, 1991 (Democrats 36-13, Republicans 32-2), the House agreed by voice vote the same day, and the President signed it December 19, 1991 [S8][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Depositors and taxpayers came out ahead with stronger protection against bank failures, and insured banks came out ahead too — they accepted higher costs but kept their federal deposit insurance guarantee with a bigger Treasury backstop behind it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Depositors and taxpayers; banks kept their guarantee

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily bipartisan at every stage: cloture passed 76-19 with both parties roughly three-quarters in favor, the House voted 398-3 to instruct conferees with zero Democratic defections, and the final Senate vote was 68-15, with Democrats splitting somewhat more (36-13) than Republicans (32-2).

industries.note: The bill charges banks more (higher assessments, annual exam fees, strict capital rules, brokered-deposit limits) but also locks in the federal deposit insurance system they operate under, enlarging the Treasury backstop behind it to $30 billion. Their cost of staying in the system rises, but the federal guarantee that underpins their deposit-taking is locked in even more firmly [S2][S3].

Thrifts face the same tighter supervision, but the law eases the qualified thrift lender test — allowing more consumer loans and more excludable liquid assets — loosening one constraint on their business. The relief comes at some cost to the discipline the rest of the bill imposes [S3].

industries.industry: Foreign banks operating in the U.S.
industries.note: Foreign banks now need Federal Reserve approval to open U.S. branches or agencies, face annual on-site exams, and must set up insured U.S. subsidiaries to take small retail deposits. Ordinary depositors gain direct regulatory oversight of institutions that previously sat partly outside it [S3].

industries.industry: Deposit brokers and high-rate deposit gatherers
industries.note: The law bars poorly capitalized banks from taking brokered deposits and caps the rates paid on them, cutting off a funding channel that had let weak institutions grow fast and fail expensively. Savers benefit through a safer insurance fund, though the restriction also limits competition for their deposits [S2][S3].

The bill delays the mandatory use of state-certified and licensed appraisers by 18 months, easing pressure on real estate transactions during the credit crunch, while new rules on real-estate-secured lending tighten bank practices. The net effect on homebuyers and the industry largely offsets [S3].
